title: Βόες ⟨τρεῖς⟩ καὶ λέων
titleEn: The Three Oxen and the Lion
part: The Three Oxen and the Lion (Chambry 71 · Perry 372)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 71 (= Perry 372). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements, [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἐνέμοντο μετ’ ἀλλήλων τρεῖς ἀεὶ βόες.
sentences.tr: Enemonto met’ allēlōn treis aei boes.
sentences.l: Three oxen always used to graze with one another.
sentences.n: ἐνέμοντο is the imperfect middle of νέμω — of animals, 'to pasture, graze'. μετ’ ἀλλήλων, 'with one another', is the reciprocal pronoun; it has no nominative, since nobody is reciprocal alone. ἀεί sets the whole fable up: the grazing together is habitual, and that is what the lion has to break.

sentences.t: Λέων δὲ τούτους φαγεῖν θέλων διὰ τὴν αὐτῶν ὁμόνοιαν οὐκ ἠδύνατο· ὑπούλοις δὲ λόγοις διαβαλὼν ἐχώρισεν ἀπ’ ἀλλήλων, καὶ τότε ἕνα ἕκαστον αὐτῶν μεμονωμένους εὑρὼν κατεθοινήσατο.
sentences.tr: Leōn de toutous phagein thelōn dia tēn autōn homonoian ouk ēdynato· hypoulois de logois diabalōn echōrisen ap’ allēlōn, kai tote hena hekaston autōn memonōmenous heurōn katethoinēsato.
sentences.l: But a lion, wishing to eat them, was not able because of their concord; and having set them at odds with insinuating words, he separated them from one another, and then, having found each one of them alone, he made a feast of them.
sentences.i: A lion wanted to eat them but could not, because they held together; so with festering words he set them against one another and parted them, and then, finding each one alone, he devoured them.
sentences.n: ὕπουλος means 'sound on the surface, festering underneath' — of a wound skinned over; ὑπούλοις λόγοις are words that look friendly and rot beneath. The two aorist participles (διαβαλών, εὑρών) with their finite verbs (ἐχώρισεν, κατεθοινήσατο) are the ordinary engine of these fables: participle for each step, one main verb for the outcome. μεμονωμένους, perfect passive participle 'having been left alone', is plural although ἕνα ἕκαστον is singular — the sense of the phrase ('each of them' = all of them, one by one) pulls the participle into the plural.

sentences.t: [Ὅτι], εἰ θέλεις μάλιστα ζῆν ἀκινδύνως, τοῖς μὲν ἐχθροῖς ἀπίστει, τοῖς δὲ φίλοις πίστευε καὶ συντήρει.
sentences.tr: [Hoti], ei theleis malista zēn akindynōs, tois men echthrois apistei, tois de philois pisteue kai syntērei.
sentences.l: [That], if you especially wish to live without danger, distrust your enemies, but trust your friends and keep them safe.
sentences.i: If you would live above all out of danger, put no trust in your enemies, but trust your friends and stand by them.
sentences.n: Chambry prints Ὅτι in square brackets, his mark for words he judges a later insertion and would delete — the text is a reconstruction, and the brackets are where the editor says so. Because he deletes it, the idiomatic line does not supply the “the story shows” that an unbracketed bare Ὅτι would take; without that word the sentence already stands on its own. The construction shifts mid-sentence: πίστευε takes the dative (τοῖς φίλοις), but συντήρει normally takes an accusative, so the second imperative is carried loosely along on the same dative.
